Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

Vignette:
Lena, a 47-year-old African woman married for over two decades, has been an architect for nearly 20 years. Her work often involves on-site visits and coordinating with construction teams, which had always provided her with both a sense of purpose and a routine she found comforting. However, everything changed six months ago when an accident at one of the sites Lena was overseeing led to serious injury to one of her colleagues. On that fateful day, Lena was inspecting safety protocols around a large piece of machinery. Despite her meticulous attention to detail, a momentary lapse in judgment allowed a mistake to slip through. The colleague she was working with was seriously injured when his hand got caught in the machine. This event triggered a cascade of traumatic responses and intrusive thoughts that have continued to plague Lena ever since. Lena describes her memories of the accident as fragmented but vivid. When she attempts to deliberately recall what happened, it feels as though the memory is just out of reach — elusive and unclear. However, when the memory does surface unexpectedly, it hits with a flood of sensory details: the metallic taste in her mouth from chewing on her tongue in shock and the sound of the machinery screeching in her mind’s ear. These vivid intrusions are often triggered by sounds reminiscent of that day, like construction noise or even the hum of an air conditioner. Lena has come to believe she is a danger to those around her, constantly monitoring for signs of potential threats even when there is no actual danger present. She finds herself jumping at ordinary sounds and having difficulty concentrating on work tasks due to these false alarms. The thought that she might cause harm again haunts her, leading to a reliance on mental rituals designed to prevent bad things from happening again. To cope with the overwhelming sense of self-blame, Lena engages in downward comparison — reminding herself it could have been worse, and focusing on how the injured colleague has recovered somewhat over time. However, this strategy is tinged with guilt as she dwells on what she believes she should have done differently. She spends hours ruminating on these failures, feeling isolated from others who seem to navigate life without such overwhelming self-doubt. Lena’s work environment has become a minefield of triggers and avoidance behaviors. She tries to avoid sites where large machinery is present and often asks colleagues to take over tasks that she perceives as potentially risky. This has strained her professional relationships, with some coworkers feeling she has become distant or overly cautious. Lena feels unrecognizable to herself; the confident architect who once thrived in fast-paced environments now finds herself second-guessing every decision. Lena is acutely aware of how different she has become since the accident. She had come to believe that her life will never be the same, and that she will always carry this burden. What frightens her most is the idea that she might cause harm again, leading her to question whether she should continue in a field where mistakes can have such severe consequences. Despite these fears, Lena has finally sought help because she recognizes that her current state of mind is unsustainable. She hopes for relief from the overwhelming self-blame and the intrusive memories, and a way back to feeling like herself again. Lena knows that continuing on this path will only lead to further isolation and professional repercussions, so she seeks support with a mix of hope and trepidation, hoping therapy can provide her with the tools to manage these distressing symptoms.
